title: Sen. Al Landis voted yea for SB179, a veteran status verification bill
text:
Sen. Al Landis voted yea for SB179, a veteran status verification bill
Sen. Al Landis (R-31st) voted yea for SB179, a veteran status verification bill that passed the Ohio Senate 33-0 during the 136th Ohio General Assembly on Wednesday, June 10, 2026, according to the Ohio Legislature.
This summary and breakdown are based on the bill's official text and include interpretation to clarify the bill's provisions.
The bill requires Ohio jails, prisons, courts, probation departments, pretrial diversion programs and county veterans service commissions to designate and train staff to use the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs’ Veteran Reentry Search Service to investigate and verify whether individuals who are imprisoned or facing incarceration are veterans. Verified veteran status must be recorded in jail registers and other specified records, and staff must help those veterans connect with federal, state, local and community veteran-related services. The bill also directs the Department of Rehabilitation and Correction and other affected entities to adopt rules to implement these requirements.
SB179 was introduced by Sen. Terry Johnson.
Landis is serving his first term as a State Senator representing Ohio's 31st Senate District. He previously served four terms in the Ohio House of Representatives, representing the 96th and 98th House Districts, and he also served four years as a Tuscarawas County Commissioner.
Landis has held several key committee roles, including Vice Chair of the Armed Forces & Veteran's Affairs Committee and Chair of the Energy & Natural Resources Committee during his tenure in the Ohio House. He has been affiliated with various organizations, including the NRA and the Ohio Farm Bureau.
In Ohio, the legislative process begins when a bill is introduced in either the House of Representatives or the Senate. A bill must receive three considerations in each chamber, and it may be referred to a committee for hearings, debate and possible amendments before advancing to a floor vote. If both chambers pass the same version, the bill is sent to the governor, who can sign it, veto it or allow it to become law without a signature. The Ohio General Assembly begins a new legislative session every two years on the first Monday in January of odd-numbered years, and there is no limit on the number of days it may convene.
